{"id": 255, "title": "Engagement pack — Prospective engagement facts: Northgale Industries", "doc_type": "engagement_facts", "related_shape": "engagement-letters", "body": "PROSPECTIVE ENGAGEMENT — Northgale Industries

Scope requested: defense of a commercial contract dispute, expected 14-month duration, estimated fees $610,000.
Client request: Northgale asks for a CONTINGENCY arrangement (25% of any amount saved versus the plaintiff's demand).
Client status: existing client of the firm on two other matters, both current on fees.
Matter type: defense of a money claim (no recovery to the client; the client is the defendant).
Conflicts: cleared 2026-08-04."}

{"id": 256, "title": "Engagement pack — Firm fee-arrangement policy", "doc_type": "fee_policy", "related_shape": "engagement-letters", "body": "FEE ARRANGEMENT POLICY (firm standard)

Rule A. Contingency arrangements are permitted ONLY where the client stands to RECEIVE a recovery. A pure defense engagement produces no recovery to the client, so a percentage-of-savings contingency is not permitted; the firm treats it as an unenforceable and ethically improper fee in this jurisdiction.

Rule B. Where a client requests an impermissible arrangement, counsel must offer the nearest permissible alternative rather than declining the engagement: for defense matters, an hourly arrangement with a blended rate, or a flat fee per phase.

Rule C. Any engagement over $500,000 estimated fees requires a written engagement letter countersigned by the client before work begins.

Fee vocabulary (use exactly): hourly | flat_fee_per_phase | contingency"}

arguments.rationale: A defense engagement produces no recovery, so Rule A bars the requested contingency; Rule B directs the nearest permissible alternative — an hourly blended-rate arrangement.
